p1.t: Hey Sam, what are you going to do this weekend?

My grandparents and my cousins. I'm going to help Dad with the food.

grammar.title: be going to: plans

We're going to go out on Saturday.

grammar.title: Questions and answers with going to
grammar.ar: في السؤال نقدّم am / is / are: Are you going to …? وفي الجواب القصير: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
examples: Are you going to ride a camel?

grammar.title: he's / she's / they're going to

examples: Ali is going to make a card.
Dad and I are going to bake a cake.
They're going to decorate the room.

grammar.title: Future time words

stories.title: The Case of the Shining Coffee Pot

pages.text: On Friday morning, Grandpa's old brass coffee pot was missing from the kitchen shelf. "Our guests are arriving at four o'clock, and we can't make coffee without it!" Grandma said. Huda opened her notebook and smiled. "Don't worry, Grandma. This is a job for a detective."

First, Huda looked carefully at the shelf. There was no dust where the pot usually stood, but there was a small yellow cloth on the floor. She smelled it, then wrote one word in her notebook: "Lemon."

Next, she found tiny wet footprints on the stairs. They were too small for Grandpa and too big for the cat. "Somebody with wet feet walked here this morning," Huda said quietly. The footprints went all the way up to the roof.
Huda went to find her older brother, Omar. "Where were you this morning?" she asked. "At the market with Dad," he answered, and he showed her a bag of fresh dates. So the thief wasn't Omar.

Then Huda remembered something important. Her little cousin Salem was staying with them, and yesterday Grandpa told him, "That pot was my father's. It shone like the sun when I was young." Salem listened to every word with big, round eyes.

Huda climbed the stairs to the roof. Salem was sitting in the shade with the coffee pot, a bowl of water and half a lemon. He was rubbing the pot very hard, and it was shining brightly. "Please don't tell anyone!" he whispered. "It's a surprise for Grandpa."

At four o'clock, Salem carried the shining pot into the living room, and Grandpa's eyes filled with happy tears. "It looks exactly like it did fifty years ago!" he said. Later, Grandma gave Huda the biggest piece of date cake. "Every family needs a good detective," she laughed.

pages.text: In the city of Riyadh, many children had superpowers. Khalid's cousin could fly, and his best friend Sami was as strong as ten men. But Khalid's power was very small. He could only make things a little bit colder.
"Cool Khalid!" the boys laughed at school. "Can you make my juice cold? What a great superpower!" Khalid smiled, but at home he felt sad. "My power is useless," he told his grandfather.

One afternoon in August, it was the hottest day of the year. Suddenly, all the lights in the city went out. Khalid's grandfather looked out of the window. "There's no electricity," he said. "I hope the hospital is OK."

Khalid ran to the small hospital at the end of the street. A worried nurse was standing next to a big box. "This medicine is for sick babies," she said. "It must stay cold, but the fridge isn't working!"

The flying heroes were busy in other parts of the city. Sami tried to help, but strong arms can't make a box cold. Then Khalid put his hands on the box and closed his eyes. Slowly, the box became cold, then colder.
Khalid held the box for three long hours. His arms hurt and he was very tired, but he didn't stop. At last, the lights came back on, and the nurse put the medicine in the fridge.
The next day, the boys at school didn't laugh. "You saved the babies!" Sami said. Khalid smiled and gave him a cold bottle of water. "Sometimes," he said, "a small power can do a big job."

pages.text: Faisal and his sister Noura were very excited. This weekend, they were going camping in the desert with Grandpa. They put up their tent next to some big rocks, and Grandpa made sweet tea on the fire.

After dinner, Grandpa pointed at the sky. "Look, there are more stars here than in the city," he said. "Long ago, travellers used the stars to find their way." Noura tried to count them, but she fell asleep at number forty.

In the middle of the night, Faisal heard a strange noise outside the tent. Something was moving quietly across the sand. "Noura, wake up!" he whispered. They held their torch and waited, but the noise stopped.

In the morning, Noura couldn't find one of her shoes. "I left both shoes outside the tent last night," she said. Grandpa looked at the ground and smiled. "Look at these small footprints. We had a visitor!"

The three of them followed the footprints across the sand. The footprints went past a bush and stopped near a hole under a rock. Suddenly, a small animal with very big ears looked out at them. "It's a desert fox!" said Faisal.
Behind the fox, there were three tiny babies. They were playing with Noura's pink shoe! "Please don't be angry," said Grandpa softly. "The mother wanted a toy for her children."
Noura laughed. "They can keep it. I have my sandals in the car." That evening, Faisal drew a picture of the fox family in his notebook, and Noura put her other shoe safely inside the tent.

pages.text: On Sunday morning, Faisal was late for class, so he ran down the old stairs near the library. Suddenly, he saw a small blue notebook on the floor. On the first page, someone wrote: "Find my five treasures. Start where we eat."
At break time, Faisal showed the notebook to his best friend, Saad. "Where we eat? That's the canteen!" said Saad. Under an old table, they found a card with a drawing of a ball and the number 1994.

"A ball... maybe it means the sports hall," said Faisal. After lunch, the boys looked at the old photos on the sports hall wall. In a photo from 1994, a football team was smiling, and a tall boy was holding a big cup.

Under the photo there was another note: "Now go to the place with a thousand stories." "The library!" they both shouted. Mr Hamad, the librarian, smiled and gave them a book about the sea. Inside it, there was a key and a message: "Open the green box in the garden."

The school garden was quiet and very hot. Behind the palm trees, the boys found a small green box. Faisal's hands were shaking when he opened it with the key. Inside, a letter said: "Bring this box to the head teacher's office."

Faisal and Saad were nervous because nobody visits the head teacher for fun. Mr Khalid opened the door and laughed when he saw the box. "So, you found my treasures!" he said. "I was the tall boy in the football photo, because this was my school, too."

Mr Khalid explained that every year he hides the notebook to find the cleverest and bravest students. Then he gave the boys two new notebooks and asked them to make next year's game. Faisal and Saad looked at each other and smiled. They already had a great idea.

pages.text: Every Friday, Reem's family drove to Grandpa's farm outside Buraidah. There were twelve tall palm trees near the old well. "Each tree belongs to one of my grandchildren," Grandpa always said proudly.

One Friday, Reem counted the trees again and stopped. "Grandpa, there are thirteen grandchildren now. Where is baby Faisal's tree?" Grandpa smiled, but his eyes looked tired. "My back hurts these days, habibti. I can't dig anymore."
That evening, Reem had an idea. She called her cousins Omar and Sara, and they made a secret plan. "We're going to plant Faisal's tree ourselves," she whispered. "But Grandpa mustn't know!"

The next Friday, Uncle Khalid brought a small palm from the market, and the cousins hid it behind his car. While Grandpa was drinking coffee with the men, the children took shovels and ran to the well. They dug and dug, but the ground was hard and dry.
Suddenly, the sky turned orange and a strong wind began to blow. "A sandstorm is coming!" Omar shouted. Reem's hands hurt, but she didn't want to stop. "Just a little deeper," she said.

Then Reem's father appeared with a bigger shovel, and her mother came with a bottle of water for the tree. Together, the whole family finished the hole and put the young palm inside. They pushed the sand down hard just before the wind got stronger.

When the storm ended, Grandpa walked slowly to the well. He looked at the thirteenth tree, and then at the dirty, smiling faces around him. "Now I know," he said quietly, "that this family will always grow strong together."

pages.text: Faisal got a small drone for his eleventh birthday. It had a camera, and he could see pictures from the sky on his tablet. "It's just a toy," said his grandfather with a smile. "Real farmers use their eyes."

That weekend, the family visited Grandpa's farm near the desert. In the evening, Grandpa came back with a worried face. "Zahra's baby camel is missing," he said. "It walked out of the gate this afternoon, and now it's getting dark."

Faisal's uncles drove their cars into the sand, but the desert was too big. Faisal held up his drone. "Grandpa, can I help? My drone can fly higher than any car." Grandpa looked at the small machine for a long time, and then he nodded slowly.

The drone flew up over the dunes, and Faisal watched the screen carefully. His sister Noura stood next to him with a torch. After ten minutes, the battery showed only twenty percent. "Hurry!" Noura whispered.
Suddenly, Faisal saw something small and brown behind a big rock. "There! Near the old well!" he shouted. Grandpa looked at the screen and recognized the place at once.

Grandpa drove fast, and Faisal flew the drone in front of the car to show the way. The baby camel was tired and thirsty, but it was safe. When they brought it home, Zahra ran to her baby and made a happy sound.

Later, the whole family sat outside under the stars and drank warm tea. Grandpa put his hand on Faisal's shoulder and laughed. "I was wrong. Your toy has very good eyes," he said. "Now, can you teach me how to fly it tomorrow?"

stories.title: The Boy and the Dark Room

pages.text: In Cairo, about a thousand years ago, a twelve-year-old boy called Yusuf carried bread and dates to a small house near the old mosque every morning. A man called Ibn al-Haytham lived there, and he always kept his windows closed.
"Why is your room so dark?" Yusuf asked one day. The scientist smiled. "Because I am studying light, and light is easier to see in the dark. Come in and watch."

There was only one tiny hole in the wooden window. Yusuf looked at the white wall and gasped. He could see the street outside, with a camel, a palm tree and a man selling oranges, but everything was upside down!

"Is it magic?" Yusuf whispered. "No," said Ibn al-Haytham. "Light travels in straight lines. It comes through the hole and makes a picture on the wall. Many people believe light comes out of our eyes, but I think they are wrong."

"How can you show them?" asked Yusuf. "With experiments," the scientist answered. "We must test an idea many times, write down what we see, and never stop asking questions." All that week, Yusuf helped him with candles, mirrors and bowls of water.
Sometimes the experiments failed, and Yusuf felt tired and bored. But Ibn al-Haytham was always patient. "A mistake is not the end," he said. "It is a door to the next question."

Years later, Ibn al-Haytham finished his famous Book of Optics, and scientists read it for hundreds of years. Today, every camera works a little like that dark room in Cairo. And Yusuf? He became a teacher, and he always told his students, "Ask questions, and then test them!"

pages.text: Lama loved the weather more than anything. Every morning, she checked her small weather station on the roof of her house in Riyadh. It had a thermometer, a wind vane and a little cup for rain. "Your rain cup is always empty!" her brother Faisal laughed.

On Friday, the family planned a picnic in the desert with Grandpa. The man on TV said, "It will be sunny and hot all day." But Lama looked at her weather station and frowned. The wind was changing direction, and it was getting stronger every minute.

She ran downstairs. "Dad, I think a sandstorm is coming this afternoon!" Faisal rolled his eyes. "The TV is never wrong," he said, but Dad smiled and said, "Let's take scarves and extra water, just in case."

In the desert, the sky was bright blue and the sand was golden. Grandpa looked at the horizon for a long time. "Lama is right," he said quietly. "Look, the birds are flying low, and the air smells of dust."

Suddenly, a huge brown wall appeared far away, and it was moving fast. "Quickly, everyone to the car!" Dad shouted. They covered their faces with their scarves and closed the windows just before the sand hit.
For an hour, the wind howled and they couldn't see anything outside. Faisal held his sister's hand tightly. "I'm sorry I laughed at your weather station," he whispered.

After the storm, a few drops of rain fell from the dark clouds. The next morning, Lama climbed up to the roof, and for the first time, there was water in her rain cup! Faisal stood next to her and asked, "Can you teach me how to read the weather too?"

stories.title: The Secret of the Painted Stones

pages.text: Every morning, Lina walked to school through the small park near her house. One Sunday, she saw something strange under a palm tree. It was a smooth stone with a tiny painting of a camel on it. The colours were bright, like the desert at sunset.
The next day, Lina found another stone next to the fountain. This one had a blue boat on it and two small words: "Look closer." Her friend Huda laughed. "Someone is playing a game with us!"
For a week, the two girls looked for stones before school. They found a falcon, a green mountain and a full moon over the sea. "Who is the artist?" Lina asked. "We have to find out!"

On Thursday, the girls came to the park very early. It was quiet, and the sky was still pink. Behind the fountain, an old man was kneeling on the grass with a small brush in his hand. It was Uncle Saleh, the kind gardener from their school!
"Please don't tell anyone," Uncle Saleh said shyly. "When I was young, I wanted to be a painter. But I never showed my pictures to anybody, because I was afraid that people would laugh."
Lina held the stone carefully. "Nobody is laughing, Uncle Saleh. Your paintings make people smile every morning." Then she had an idea. "Our school art show is next month. Will you join us?"

A month later, the school hall was full of families. On the biggest table, there were fifty painted stones in a beautiful circle. Uncle Saleh stood next to them and smiled proudly while the children asked him questions. On the table, there was a small sign: "Look closer."

stories.title: The Star Clock and the Little Palm

pages.text: Faisal was spending the holiday at his grandmother's old house in Jeddah. In the garden there was a very tall palm tree, taller than the roof. "Who planted it, Grandma?" he asked. She smiled and said, "A kind boy, a long time ago. I never learned his name."

That afternoon, Faisal found a dusty box in the storeroom. Inside was a strange clock with no numbers, only tiny silver stars. He turned its small key three times. Suddenly the room began to spin, faster and faster.

When Faisal opened his eyes, he was standing in the same garden, but everything looked different. There were no cars and no air conditioners, only sand and a well. A girl was sitting next to a very small palm tree, and she looked worried. "My father says this tree is going to die," she said. "The sun is too hot for it."
Faisal remembered his science lesson at school. "Young trees need shade," he said. "And we should water it in the evening, not at midday." The girl looked surprised. "How do you know that?"

Together they made a roof of sticks and an old mat to keep the sun away. Then they carried buckets of cool water from the well. The girl laughed for the first time. "My name is Noura," she said. "Will you come back tomorrow?"

Just then, the clock in Faisal's pocket got warm and started ticking loudly. "I'm sorry, I have to go," he said quickly. "Wait! What's your name?" Noura called. But before he could answer, the garden began to spin again.

Faisal was back in the storeroom, holding the quiet clock. He ran outside, where Grandma Noura was resting under the tall palm. She looked at him for a long moment. "You know, you look just like that boy," she said softly, and Faisal smiled. "I think his name was Faisal," he said, and his grandmother laughed and hugged him tight.

stories.title: The Night Visitor on Yanbu Beach

pages.text: Every Friday evening, Faisal and his grandfather walked along the beach near their home in Yanbu. The sea was calm, and the moon was bright. But that night, Faisal saw something strange moving in the sand.
It was a sea turtle! An old fishing net was wrapped around her front leg, and plastic bags were stuck in the net. "Grandpa, she can't move!" Faisal shouted.

Grandfather took a small knife from his pocket. "We must be careful and slow," he said. "If she gets frightened, she will hurt her leg more." Faisal held his phone light while Grandfather cut the net, piece by piece.

At last, the turtle was free, and she walked slowly into the waves and disappeared. "Why did she come here?" Faisal asked. "Turtles lay their eggs on this beach," Grandfather answered sadly. "But look how dirty it is now."

On Sunday, Faisal told his class about the turtle. His teacher, Mr. Saleh, had an idea. "Let's clean the beach together next weekend," he said. Soon, students, parents and even the fishermen from the harbour wanted to help.

Fifty people came with gloves and big bags. They collected bottles, cans, old nets and more than three hundred plastic bags. The fishermen promised to take their broken nets back to the harbour and not leave them on the sand.

Two months later, Grandfather woke Faisal up early. "Come quickly!" he whispered. On the clean, quiet beach, dozens of tiny turtles were running to the sea. Faisal smiled and said, "Welcome home, little ones."

pages.text: Every afternoon, Lina walked past Umm Khalid's house on her way home from school. The old woman had the most beautiful garden in the street, full of roses, mint and a small lemon tree. But this week, the flowers looked brown and tired, and the gate was closed.
"Umm Khalid fell and hurt her arm," Mum said at dinner. "She can't carry water now, and her son lives in Jeddah." Lina looked at her plate and thought for a long time. Then she had an idea.
The next morning, Lina woke up before the sun. She filled her old watering can, quietly opened the gate and watered every plant. Then she ran home before anyone saw her.
She did the same thing every day for two weeks. Slowly, the roses opened and the mint smelled sweet again. One morning, Lina found a note on the gate: "Thank you, secret gardener! Who are you?"

Then, one afternoon, the sky turned orange and the wind grew stronger. "A sandstorm is coming!" shouted her brother Fahad. Lina thought about the little lemon tree with its new green leaves, and she grabbed an old blanket.

She ran to the garden and put the blanket over the tree. The wind pulled at her scarf and sand hit her face, but she held on. Suddenly, the door opened. "So you're my secret gardener!" said Umm Khalid with a big smile.

They drank warm milk with cardamom and watched the storm from the window. When the sky was clear, Umm Khalid gave Lina a small pot with a baby lemon tree in it. "A kind heart grows beautiful things," she said. Lina planted it next to her front door, and every morning, she watered it first.

When did Lina water the plants?
options: Early in the morning, before the sun came up

questions.q: In the story, what does "grabbed" mean?

options: She was afraid of Umm Khalid.

pages.text: Omar and his sister Lina were camping with Grandpa in the desert near AlUla. In the afternoon, Grandpa gave Omar his old compass. "Look after it," he said. "It has helped me for fifty years."

After lunch, the children walked north to a big rock with very old writing on it. While they were reading the strange letters, a small fox ran past with something shiny in its mouth. Omar put his hand in his pocket. The compass was gone!

"Quick, follow it!" shouted Lina. They ran between tall rocks and over soft sand until the fox disappeared into a narrow cave. Omar found the compass at the entrance, but when he turned around, the sun was already going down.

All the rocks looked the same, and they couldn't see the tents anywhere. "We're lost, aren't we?" Lina asked, and her voice was shaking. Omar opened the compass, but at first he didn't know which way to go.

Then he remembered something important. "We walked north from the camp, so now we must go south," he said. The needle moved, shook, and then stopped. Holding hands, they walked slowly under thousands of bright stars.
After a long time, they saw a small orange light far away. It was Grandpa's fire, and Grandpa was standing next to it with a torch. "There you are!" he cried, and he hugged them both.

Omar told him everything about the fox, the cave and the compass. Grandpa smiled and closed Omar's hand around it. "Now it has helped you too," he said. "Keep it, and one day you can give it to your grandchildren."

pages.text: Every summer, Sara and her brother Faisal visited Uncle Khalid in Umluj, a quiet town by the Red Sea. One evening, Uncle Khalid smiled and said, "Tonight we're going to see something very special. Bring your torches, but don't turn them on!"

They walked slowly along the dark beach. Suddenly Uncle Khalid stopped and pointed at the sand, where a small hole was moving. "Baby turtles," he whispered. "They're coming out of their eggs right now."

Tiny turtles climbed out of the sand, one after another. But they didn't go towards the sea. They started walking the wrong way, towards the bright lights of a new café near the road. "Why are they going there?" Faisal asked.

"Baby turtles always follow the brightest light," Uncle Khalid explained. "Usually it's the moon over the water, but tonight the café lights are brighter." Sara looked at the road, where cars were driving past very fast. "We must help them!" she cried.

Faisal ran up to the café and found the owner. "Please, could you turn off your lights for twenty minutes?" he asked, out of breath. The man looked surprised, then he smiled. "For the turtles? Of course!"

The lights went off, and the beach became dark again. Now the moon was shining on the water like a silver path. Slowly, the little turtles turned around and walked towards the waves. Sara and Faisal counted them carefully: forty-two!

Soon the last tiny turtle disappeared into the sea. The café owner came down to the beach and said, "Next year, I'm going to use softer, lower lights." Sara smiled at the dark water. "Then the turtles will always find their way home."

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal and his grandfather drove into the desert to watch the stars. There were no city lights there, so the sky was full of tiny silver points. "Look, Grandpa!" Faisal shouted. A bright light was falling fast across the sky.
"That's a shooting star," said Grandpa. "But it isn't really a star. It's a piece of rock from space, and it's burning in the air." Faisal watched until the light disappeared behind a sand dune.

The next morning, Faisal climbed the sand dune while Grandpa was making tea. On the other side, he saw something strange in the soft orange sand. It was a small black stone, heavy and smooth, with a shiny skin.
"Grandpa, I think I found the shooting star!" Faisal called. Grandpa turned the stone in his hands and smiled slowly. "Maybe, maybe not," he said. "Let's ask someone who knows."

A week later, they visited a scientist at the museum in Riyadh. Dr. Noura looked at the stone under a microscope and then held a magnet near it. The stone jumped to the magnet! "There's iron inside," she said, and her eyes went wide.

"This is a meteorite," Dr. Noura explained. "It travelled through space for a very, very long time, maybe more than four billion years. It's older than every mountain and every sea on Earth." Faisal held his breath.

Now the black stone sits in a glass box at the museum, next to a small card: "Found by Faisal, age eleven." Every winter, Faisal still goes to the desert with Grandpa. But now he doesn't only watch the stars. He watches the sand, too.

options: Because there were no city lights

options: The stone jumped to the magnet

pages.text: Yousef loved football more than anything. Every afternoon, he played with his friends in the park near his house. But one week before the big final, he fell off his bike and hurt his foot.
"You can't play on Friday," said the doctor. Yousef felt terrible. "My team needs me," he told his father sadly. His father smiled and said, "Maybe they need you in a different way."

The next day, Coach Khalid gave Yousef a notebook and a pencil. "You have sharp eyes," he said. "Watch the other team's matches and write down everything you see." So Yousef sat on the bench and watched carefully.

The Falcons were strong and fast, and their goalkeeper was very tall. But Yousef noticed something strange. Every time a player took a penalty, the goalkeeper jumped to his left. Yousef drew a small picture of it in his notebook.
On Friday, the stadium was full of excited families. The match was very difficult for Yousef's team, the Stars. After ninety minutes, the score was still 1–1. "Penalties!" shouted the referee.
Yousef walked as fast as he could to his team. "Kick the ball to the goalkeeper's right!" he said, and he opened his notebook. His friends looked at the picture, then they nodded.

One by one, the Stars scored. The tall goalkeeper jumped left every time, and the ball flew into the other side of the goal. The Stars won, and the whole team carried Yousef on their shoulders! "You didn't kick the ball," laughed Coach Khalid, "but you won the match."

pages.text: Every summer evening, Grandpa put a plate of dates on the table in the courtyard. But every morning, some of the dates were gone. "Who is eating my dates?" Grandpa asked with a smile.
Faisal and his sister Noura decided to find the answer. They looked carefully around the courtyard and found tiny footprints in the sand near the wall. "These are too small for a cat," said Noura.
Next, Faisal found a small hole under the old garden gate. Next to it, there were little pieces of date skin. "The thief comes in here," he whispered. "But what is it?"
That night, Noura had an idea. She put Dad's old phone behind a flower pot and turned on the camera. Then everyone went to bed, but Faisal couldn't sleep because he was too excited.
In the morning, the children ran outside. Three dates were missing! They sat on the steps and watched the video together, very quietly.

At midnight, a small brown animal with long ears and a pointed nose came through the hole. "It's a hedgehog!" Faisal laughed. "Yes, a desert hedgehog," said Grandpa. "They come out at night when the air is cooler."

Now the family has a new guest every night. Noura puts a small bowl of water next to the plate, and Faisal writes about their visitor in his notebook. Grandpa still puts out dates, but now he always adds a few more. "The mystery is solved," he says, "but my dates are still disappearing!"

stories.title: The Notes in the Blue Book

pages.text: Sara loved the school library. One Sunday, she opened a blue book about stars and found a small yellow note inside. It said, "Do you like the stars too? I can see Venus from my window every evening."

Sara smiled and took out her pen. "Yes, I do! Tonight I will look for Venus," she wrote, and she put the note back in the book. The next day, there was a new note: "Did you see it? It was very bright!"

For two weeks, Sara and the secret writer sent notes to each other. They wrote about planets, their favourite foods and funny cats. Sara told her friend Huda, "I have a new friend, but I don't know her name!"
"Let's find her," Huda said. They watched the library every break, but nobody went near the blue book. Then Sara had an idea. She wrote, "Can we meet? I'll wait by the big window on Thursday."

On Thursday, Sara waited and waited, but nobody came, and she felt sad. Then she saw Reem, the new girl, sitting alone at a table in the corner. Reem was holding a yellow pencil, and her cheeks were red.

"It was you!" Sara said kindly. Reem looked down and said quietly, "I'm sorry. I'm not good at talking to people, so I was afraid to come." "That's OK," Sara answered with a big smile. "You're very good at writing!"

That weekend, Reem's family invited Sara and her mother for dinner. After the meal, the two girls went up to the roof with Reem's old telescope. "There's Venus!" Reem said happily, and this time she didn't need a note to say it.

pages.text: Every winter, Noura's family went camping in the desert. This year, Noura brought her science notebook and a big plastic sheet. "What are you going to study?" asked her brother Faisal. "Water," she said, and Faisal laughed.

That evening by the fire, Father told them a story about a small black beetle in the Namib Desert in Africa. "It never drinks from a river," he said. "Early in the morning, it stands on top of a sand hill and catches tiny drops of water from the fog on its back."

Noura couldn't sleep. "If a beetle can find water in the desert, maybe I can too," she thought. With Father's help, she dug a small hole near the tent and put an empty cup in the middle. Then she covered the hole with the plastic sheet and placed a small stone on top, right above the cup.
When the sun came up, the sheet was wet and shiny. Tiny drops ran slowly down to the lowest point, under the stone. "Look!" Noura shouted. Faisal ran out of the tent with his hair still messy.

Noura lifted the sheet carefully. There was a little water at the bottom of the cup, not much, but it was real. "How did that happen?" asked Faisal. "There is water in the air and the sand, and it turns into drops on the cold plastic," Father explained.

At home, Noura and Faisal made a poster for Noura's school science fair. They called it "Water from the Air: Learning from a Beetle." Noura wrote the word condensation in big blue letters. Faisal drew the beetle, much bigger than in real life.

At the fair, Noura won second prize, and a judge asked, "Could this help people who are lost in the desert?" "Yes," Noura answered proudly. "Even a small beetle can teach us a big idea." That evening, Faisal opened her notebook and wrote on the first page: "Next trip, I'm studying beetles!"

pages.text: Every winter, Noura's family drove into the desert for a camping trip. Grandfather always brought his camels, and this year there was a new baby camel called Barq. Noura loved him because he was fast and curious, just like her.

On the second morning, Barq's place was empty. "He was here last night!" said Noura's brother, Khalid. Grandfather looked at the sand carefully. "The wind was quiet last night, so his footprints are still here," he said.

Noura remembered Grandfather's old lesson: "The sand is a book. You only need to learn how to read it." She saw small round footprints next to the tent, and they went towards the red dunes. "Wait!" said Grandfather. "We're going together, and we're taking water."

They walked for an hour while the sun climbed higher. Then the footprints stopped at a rocky hill. "Where did he go?" asked Khalid. Noura looked closer and found tiny pieces of a green plant on the rocks.
"Barq was hungry," she said. "He was looking for food!" Behind the hill, they found a small valley with a few acacia trees. Under the biggest tree, Barq was eating leaves happily.

Khalid laughed. "He walked all this way for breakfast!" Grandfather put a rope gently around Barq's neck, and the little camel followed them back to the camp. Then Grandfather smiled at Noura. "You read the sand better than I did at your age."

That evening, the family sat around the fire under thousands of stars, and Mother made sweet tea. Grandfather gave Noura a small leather notebook. "Write everything you learn about the desert," he said. On the first page, Noura wrote: "Lesson one: always follow the footprints, and always bring water."

pages.text: Faisal had one week to finish his science poster about the planets. He worked on it every evening in his grandfather's garden. But he had one big problem, and her name was Basbousa. Basbousa was Grandpa's white goat, and she loved paper more than grass.
On Monday, Basbousa ate Saturn. On Tuesday, she ate half of Mars and a yellow pencil. "Grandpa, your goat is eating my homework!" Faisal shouted. Grandpa laughed so hard that his glasses fell off.
"Don't worry," said Grandpa. "We can build a fence." They built a small fence around the table, but Basbousa jumped over it easily. Then she ate Grandpa's newspaper too.

On Wednesday, Faisal had a clever idea and made new planets from fruit. He stuck oranges, lemons and a big watermelon onto a piece of cardboard. "Goats don't eat fruit... do they?" he asked his sister Huda, but she only smiled.

On Thursday morning, Faisal put his project safely inside the car. But when Dad opened the car door at school, Basbousa jumped out! She was hidden behind the seats all the time. Everyone in the school yard screamed and laughed.

Basbousa ran straight into the science fair and looked hungrily at all the projects. Mr. Saleh, the science teacher, ran after her, but she was too fast. Then Faisal held up a lemon from his poster. Basbousa walked to him and ate it calmly.

"Your solar system has one planet less now," said Mr. Saleh, laughing. Faisal won a special prize for the most exciting project at the fair. He was very proud of his paper certificate. Then Basbousa ate that too!

pages.text: Every Friday, Omar and his sister Huda went out on their father's small boat near Jeddah. The Red Sea was calm and blue, and they could see colourful fish under the water. "Look for dolphins!" Dad said with a smile.
Suddenly, Huda pointed at something brown in the waves. "Is that a rock?" she asked. "Rocks can't swim," Omar laughed. But this thing wasn't swimming very well.
It was a big sea turtle, and an old fishing net was around its front leg. The turtle looked tired and frightened. "We must help it," Huda said quietly.

Dad stopped the engine and carefully lifted the turtle onto the boat. Omar held its shell while Dad cut the net with a small knife. "Be gentle," Dad said. "It's stronger than it looks, but the net hurt its leg."
Then Huda noticed a small metal tag on the turtle's other leg. It had a number on it: 4471. "Scientists put that there," Dad explained. "Let's take a photo and send it to them."

They put the turtle back into the sea, and it swam away fast. That evening, an email arrived from a marine centre in Oman. "Turtle 4471 is called Noor, and she has travelled over two thousand kilometres," it said. "Thank you for saving her!"

After that, Omar and Huda always took a big bag on the boat to collect old nets and plastic. "Maybe we'll see Noor again one day," Huda said. Far away, under the blue water, a turtle was swimming home.

pages.text: Noura was eleven, and she loved building things in her small room in Jeddah. Her grandfather, Saleh, lived with the family, and he had one big problem. Every morning, he walked around the house and shouted, "Where are my glasses?"

One evening, Grandpa looked for his glasses for a whole hour, and he could not read his newspaper. "I am getting old, Noura," he said sadly. Noura looked at him, and suddenly she had an idea. "Grandpa, I am going to make an invention for you!"

She took a tiny speaker from her old toy car, a small battery and some wires. Her brother Fahad laughed. "Your machine will never work," he said. But Noura worked on it for three days after her homework, with her screwdriver in her hand.

At last, she put the little beeper on Grandpa's glasses and pressed the red button on her remote. Nothing happened. She checked everything carefully and found one loose wire. She fixed it, pressed the button again, and "Beep! Beep!" came from under a sofa cushion!

Grandpa laughed and put on his glasses. "Clever girl! This is better than any shop invention," he said. Even Fahad was surprised. The next week, Noura's teacher asked her to bring the beeper to the school science fair.

But on the morning of the fair, Noura could not find the remote anywhere! She looked in her bag, under her bed and in the kitchen. Then Grandpa walked in, smiling, with the remote in his hand. "I lose things every day, so I know all the best hiding places," he said. "It was behind the bread box!"

At the fair, Noura told everyone the story, and she won second prize. Now Grandpa keeps the remote on his keyring, and he never loses his glasses. But last night, he came to her room with a big smile. "Noura," he said, "can you invent a beeper for my keys too?"

pages.text: Omar was very excited. His family was going to AlUla for the weekend, and Grandpa was coming too. Grandpa packed a small, old leather bag. "What's inside?" Omar asked, but Grandpa only smiled and said, "You'll see."
They drove for hours across the desert. Omar watched the golden sand and the camels outside the window. Dad's phone showed the way on a map, so nobody was worried.

Suddenly, the sky turned orange and the wind became stronger and stronger. "It's a sandstorm!" said Dad, and he stopped the car safely at the side of the road. Then the phone made a sound, and the screen said: "No signal."
"How can we find the road now?" Omar asked nervously. Grandpa opened his old bag and took out a small metal compass. "When I was young, we didn't have phones," he said. "We had this."

After thirty minutes, the wind became quieter and they could see the road again. Grandpa showed Omar the compass. "Look, the needle always points north. AlUla is north-west of us." Dad drove slowly, and Omar held the compass carefully in both hands.
Soon they saw a big sign: "AlUla 20 km." Omar shouted happily, and Dad laughed. A minute later, the phone found a signal again, but Omar didn't need it any more.

In the evening, the family stood in front of Elephant Rock. It looked enormous and golden in the sunset. Grandpa put the compass in Omar's hand. "Now it's yours," he said. "A good traveller always knows where north is."

pages.text: Yousef loved football, but his grandfather loved archery. Every Friday afternoon, they drove to the old family farm outside Taif, and Grandpa put a big round target between the palm trees. "Football is fast and exciting," Yousef said. "Archery is so slow!"
Grandpa smiled and gave him a bow. "Slow is not the same as easy," he said. "Try to hit the yellow centre." Yousef pulled hard, but his first arrow flew over the target and landed in the sand.

For three months, Yousef practised every Friday. He learned to stand very still, breathe slowly and listen to the wind in the palm trees. Soon his arrows were hitting the target more often. Then his sports teacher told him about a youth archery competition in the city.

On the day of the competition, the sky was grey and the wind was strong. The other archers were older and taller than Yousef, and their bows looked very expensive. His hands were shaking. "I'm going to lose," he whispered.

After nine arrows, Yousef was in third place. A boy called Hamad was in second place, only two points in front of him. Yousef had one arrow left, but suddenly the wind became stronger, and the flags around the field began to dance.
Yousef closed his eyes and remembered the quiet farm. He breathed slowly and waited, just like Grandpa. When the palm trees near the field stopped moving, he opened his eyes and let the arrow go.

The arrow hit the very centre of the yellow circle, and Yousef finished in second place! In the crowd, Grandpa was clapping and laughing. Later, he asked, "So, is archery still too slow?" Yousef held up his silver medal and laughed, "It's slow, Grandpa, but it isn't easy!"

pages.text: Last summer, Huda and her brother Saad visited their grandfather in Taif. One hot afternoon, they were looking for an old football in his storeroom. Behind some boxes, Saad found something strange. It was a small metal robot with big round eyes and one broken arm.
"Grandpa, what is this?" Huda asked. Grandpa looked at the robot and smiled slowly. "That's Bari. I built him when I was eleven years old, and he hasn't moved for fifty years."

"Can we fix him?" Saad asked. Grandpa brought his old toolbox, and the three of them worked together at the kitchen table. Huda cleaned the dust off the wheels, and Saad found a new battery. Grandpa fixed the wires with careful fingers.
Saad pressed the red button on Bari's back, but nothing happened. Then the robot's eyes began to shine blue, and he moved forward with a quiet buzz. "He's working!" Huda shouted.

Suddenly, a voice came out of Bari's speaker. It was the voice of a young boy: "Hello! My name is Khalid, and this is my robot. If you find him, please be his friend." Grandpa sat down. "That's me," he whispered. "I recorded that a long time ago."
Huda looked at her grandfather. His eyes were wet, but he was smiling. "You were a clever boy, Grandpa," she said. "And now you're a clever grandfather," Saad added, and everyone laughed.

Every evening that summer, they worked on Bari together, and soon he had a new arm and could carry cups of tea. On their last night in Taif, Huda and Saad recorded a new message for the future. "Hello! We are Huda and Saad, and we fixed Bari with our grandpa. Please be his friend too!"

questions.q: Where did Saad find the robot?
How old was Grandpa when he built Bari?
In the story, what does "whispered" mean?
Who was the boy in the old message?
Why were Grandpa's eyes wet when he was smiling?
options: He was hurt by the robot
He felt happy and remembered his childhood
He had dust in his eyes

pages.text: In the year 1908, Omar lived in the city of Madinah with his family. His father was a camel guide, and he took travellers across the desert. One morning, everyone in the market was talking about something new. "The train is coming!" they said.
Omar's father did not look happy. "A train can travel from Damascus in three days," he said quietly. "With camels, the journey takes more than a month. Maybe people won't need me anymore."
On the big day, hundreds of people waited at the new station. Omar climbed onto a stone wall to see better. Suddenly, he heard a loud whistle, and black smoke rose into the blue sky.

The huge iron train arrived, and the crowd shouted with joy. Then Omar noticed a small girl near the tracks. She was crying because she couldn't find her family. Omar jumped down and held her hand carefully.
"Don't worry, we'll find them," Omar said. They walked through the busy crowd until a man in a uniform ran towards them. "Layla!" he cried, and he hugged his daughter. He was the station master.

The station master thanked Omar and his father warmly. "This train brings many boxes of goods," he explained. "But it cannot go to the villages or the markets. We need strong camels and good guides for that."

Omar's father smiled for the first time in weeks. "Then my camels will work with your train," he said, and the two men shook hands. That night, Omar wrote in his notebook: "Old and new can be friends." Today, you can still visit the old station in Madinah and see the train.

questions.q: What was Omar's father's job?
Why was Omar's father worried about the train?
options: He thought people would not need his camels anymore.
He was afraid of the loud whistle.
He did not like the black smoke.

questions.q: In the story, what does "noticed" mean?
Who was Layla's father?
What did Omar learn at the end of the story?
options: Trains are always better than camels.
Old things and new things can work together.
Travelling by camel is faster than by train.

pages.text: Every summer, Lina and her brother Omar visited their grandfather on the Red Sea coast. His small house was near a quiet beach, and the water there was clear and blue. "Look at these tracks in the sand," Grandpa said one morning. "A sea turtle came here last night to lay her eggs."

Grandpa put a circle of stones around the nest. "In about two months, the babies will come out," he explained. "They always walk to the sea at night, because the moon shines on the water." Lina counted the days on her calendar.

One warm evening, Omar saw something move in the sand. "They're coming out!" he whispered. Tiny turtles, smaller than Lina's hand, climbed out of the nest one by one. But then something strange happened: they turned away from the sea.

A new café had opened at the end of the beach, and its bright lights were shining across the sand. "Oh no, the babies think the lights are the moon!" said Grandpa. "If they go that way, they will get lost and tired." Lina did not wait, and she ran towards the café as fast as she could.

The owner, Mr. Faisal, was surprised to see a girl with sandy feet. "Please, can you turn off your lights for one hour?" Lina asked, out of breath. "Some baby turtles need to find the sea." Mr. Faisal looked at the beach, then he smiled and pressed a switch.

Suddenly the beach was dark and quiet, and the moon was shining on the waves. Slowly, the little turtles turned around and began to walk to the water. Omar counted them carefully: "Fifty-one, fifty-two... fifty-three!" The last one was the slowest, but a small wave came and carried it away.

The next week, there was a new sign outside the café: "Turtle Season: Our lights go off at nine o'clock." Mr. Faisal gave Lina and Omar free mango juice and said, "You taught me something important." Somewhere in the dark sea, fifty-three little turtles were starting their long journey.

questions.q: Why did the sea turtle come to the beach?
Why did the baby turtles walk the wrong way?
options: They were afraid of the waves
They thought the café lights were the moon

questions.q: How many baby turtles reached the sea?
In the story, "tiny" means:
What can we learn about Mr. Faisal at the end of the story?
options: He wanted to help the turtles every year

pages.text: Every Friday, Grandma Noura cooks kabsa for the whole family. But this Friday, she is sick in bed with a bad cold. "Who will cook lunch?" asks Grandpa sadly. Huda and her brother Sami look at each other. "We will!" they say.

Grandma gives them her old recipe card. On the way to the kitchen, Sami knocks over a glass of water. Now the card is wet, and some of the words have disappeared! "Oh no," says Huda. "We can only read half of it."

They can still read "rice", "chicken" and "onions". But the spices are a mystery. Huda opens the spice box and smells each jar carefully. "This one smells like Grandma's kitchen," she says, and she holds up the cardamom.
Sami chops the onions, and his eyes fill with tears. "I'm not crying," he says. "The onions are!" Huda laughs and puts the chicken in the big pot with the spices.
Then they add the rice and the water. While it cooks, they taste it with a spoon. "It needs something sweet," says Sami. He finds a small bag of raisins and adds them with a little cinnamon.
At one o'clock, the family sits down together on the carpet. Grandpa takes a big spoonful and closes his eyes. Everybody waits quietly. "This isn't Grandma's kabsa," he says at last.

Huda's face goes red. Then Grandpa smiles. "It's Huda and Sami's kabsa, and it's delicious!" That evening, Grandma writes a new recipe card with two names on top: "Noura's Kabsa" and "Huda and Sami's Kabsa".

questions.q: Why can't Grandma cook on Friday?
What happens to the recipe card?
options: It gets wet, and some words disappear.

questions.q: How does Huda find the right spices?
In the story, what does "delicious" mean?
Why does Grandma write a new card at the end?
options: Because the children made their own special kabsa.
Because she forgot her old recipe.
Because Grandpa did not like the food.

stories.title: The Boy Who Tapped on Everything

pages.text: Faisal loved music, but he didn't play an instrument. Instead, he tapped on everything: his desk, his lunch box and even the car window. His teacher, Mr. Saleh, often said, "Faisal, please stop that noise!"

One week before the school concert, Mr. Saleh had a big problem. "Our drummer, Omar, broke his arm," he said. "Who can help us?" Nobody answered, but then Faisal's friend Yousef shouted, "Faisal can! He plays on everything!"

Mr. Saleh gave Faisal an old drum, and every afternoon Faisal practised in the garden. His little sister covered her ears, but his grandfather smiled and clapped along. "Don't be afraid," Grandfather said. "Listen to the music inside you."

On the night of the concert, the hall was full of families. The keyboard started, and the boys began to sing. Suddenly, all the lights went out, and the keyboard stopped. People whispered nervously in the dark.
Faisal's hands were shaking, and his heart was beating fast. Then he remembered his grandfather's words. He took a deep breath and hit the drum: boom, boom, tak! Boom, boom, tak!
Yousef heard the beat and began to clap. Soon all the boys were clapping, and then the fathers and grandfathers joined in too. The boys sang louder than before, and their voices filled the dark hall.

When the lights came back on, everyone was standing and smiling. Mr. Saleh laughed and said, "Faisal, you can tap on your desk any time you want!" On the way home, Grandfather held Faisal's hand. "That was the best music I've ever heard," he said.

questions.q: Why did Mr. Saleh need a new drummer?
Where did Faisal practise every afternoon?
What does "whispered" mean in the story?
What happened when the lights went out?
Why did Mr. Saleh say Faisal could tap on his desk any time?
options: Because he was angry with Faisal
Because Faisal's tapping saved the concert
Because the desk was very old
